facts.fact: Blender manual: Random Walk (Skin) is a Cycles-only subsurface method tuned for skin; per the search snippet of the current Principled BSDF page, its radius is automatically adjusted based on the color texture (snippet-level, not verified against full page text).

Blender manual gives skin as an example subsurface anisotropy value and states skin has been measured at anisotropy 0.8 (the manual cites this value; primary measurement study not verified in this run).
Subsurface anisotropy of 0 means uniform scattering direction inside the medium.
Subsurface Radius is the average distance light scatters below the surface, with separate RGB values per channel, so red can scatter deeper than blue.
Subsurface Scale is a multiplier on the radius; its slider range is documented as 0 to 50 cm.
Subsurface IOR is used for rays entering the subsurface component, is Cycles-only, and may differ from the global IOR (the manual suggests this for simulating skin layers).
Global IOR: the manual states most materials fall between 1.0 (vacuum/air) and 4.0 (germanium), with default 1.5 approximating glass.
Specular Anisotropy is a Cycles-only input: positive values elongate highlights along the tangent direction, negative values shape highlights perpendicular to the tangent.
In thin-wall mode, the Subsurface Radius, Subsurface Scale and Subsurface Method inputs have no effect.

Blender 3.6 manual lists Random Walk modes under Subsurface Method with radius modulated by color, and uses older input names such as 'Subsurface Anisotropy' and 'Anisotropic'; names changed in later versions.

Blender developer PR #110989 explains the skin random-walk mode randomly chooses between diffuse Lambertian transmission and GGX refraction at fixed roughness 1; diffuse is mixed in because a pure random walk penetrates too deep into skin.
Forum practitioner claim: Random Walk (skin) yields results similar to the older random walk but loses the surface roughness control because it fixes roughness at 1.

Forum claim: Random Walk (skin) lacks the scaling the legacy random walk applies to approximate Burley; a forum post says Blender 5.2 splits the random-walk options into legacy and newer variants. Not confirmed in official docs.

Forum practitioner opinion: random walk with zero anisotropy can look fake, lacking a thin film of surface detail; another poster argues radius and color adjustments matter more than anisotropy for a close match.
Forum-reported artifact: Subsurface Scattering can produce flat-shaded artifacts on some meshes, a known practical issue.

Random Walk uses volumetric scattering inside the mesh, so overlapping faces and holes/open meshes can cause errors; closed meshes work best (manual-derived statement from the Principled search results).

contradictions: Manual snippet says Random Walk (Skin) radius is auto-adjusted by color texture, while a forum post says Random Walk (skin) lacks the Burley-approximating scaling of the legacy random walk; these describe different aspects and were not reconciled against the full manual text.

Forum claims about Blender 5.2 splitting random-walk modes (legacy vs new) conflict with the 5.3 manual excerpt, which lists the modes differently; version naming is inconsistent across manual pages (3.4 'Random Walk (Fixed Radius)', 4.x 'Random Walk (Legacy)' in a non-English page).
Forum statement that random walk costs more render time and noise for dense media like skin is attributed to Blender docs by a forum post, but not located in the docs pages retrieved.
